cards.q: What is SNMP and which ports does it use?
cards.a: SNMP monitors and manages network devices; UDP 161 carries requests/responses and UDP 162 carries notifications such as traps and informs. Major versions are SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, and SNMPv3, with v3 preferred for security.

cards.q: What are the roles of the SNMP manager and agent?
cards.a: The manager is the network-management system that polls devices, collects statistics, and sends SET operations when authorized; the agent runs on the managed device, maintains managed information, responds to requests, and generates notifications.

cards.q: What is the difference between a MIB and an OID?
cards.a: A MIB (Management Information Base) defines the managed objects that can be monitored/managed and is organized hierarchically; an OID (Object Identifier) identifies a specific object in that hierarchy.

cards.q: What are the common OID branches and the Cisco enterprise OID?
cards.a: 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 is System, .2.1.2 is Interfaces, .2.1.4 is IP, 1.3.6.1.4.1 is private enterprise, and the Cisco enterprise branch is 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.

cards.q: What are the SNMP operations?
cards.a: GET reads a specific object, GETNEXT retrieves the next object in the MIB tree, GETBULK efficiently retrieves multiple objects, SET modifies an object, TRAP is an unsolicited notification, and INFORM is a notification requiring acknowledgment.

cards.q: Which SNMP version introduced GETBULK?
cards.a: GETBULK was introduced with SNMPv2 and is not an SNMPv1 operation.

cards.q: What is the difference between a TRAP and an INFORM?
cards.a: Both are unsolicited, agent-initiated notifications, but a trap is not acknowledged while an inform requires the manager to send an acknowledgment; informs are more reliable but still normally use UDP.

cards.q: What are the security characteristics of SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c?
cards.a: Both use community strings with no encryption and no strong cryptographic authentication; the c in v2c means community-based security.

cards.q: What did SNMPv2c add over v1?
cards.a: GETBULK and INFORM, plus better protocol operations, but it retained community-based security rather than modern cryptographic security.

cards.q: What are the three SNMPv3 security levels?
cards.a: noAuthNoPriv (no authentication, no encryption), authNoPriv (authentication, no encryption), and authPriv (authentication plus encryption/privacy), which is generally preferred.

cards.q: What do the SNMPv3 security levels mean in practice?
cards.a: noAuthNoPriv authenticates no one and encrypts nothing; authNoPriv verifies message origin but leaves the payload readable; authPriv authenticates and encrypts SNMP messages.

cards.q: Which algorithms does SNMPv3 commonly use for authentication and privacy?
cards.a: Authentication commonly uses MD5 or SHA variants; privacy/encryption commonly uses DES or AES variants, with stronger algorithms preferred when supported.

cards.q: What are SNMP community strings, and why are they dangerous?
cards.a: They are v1/v2c access credentials such as RO (read-only) and RW (read-write); they are not encryption and should not be treated as secure passwords, especially RW which can allow unauthorized modification.

cards.q: What are the basic SNMPv2c configuration commands?
cards.a: snmp-server community cisco123 RO, snmp-server community netops RW (read-write, avoid if not required), snmp-server host 10.0.0.5 version 2c cisco123, snmp-server location R1, and snmp-server contact netadmin@corp.

cards.q: What are the main steps of an SNMPv3 configuration?
cards.a: Create a group (snmp-server group ADMIN v3 priv), create a user with auth and privacy (snmp-server user cisco-user ADMIN v3 auth sha SecretAuth priv aes 128 SecretPriv), and set the notification destination (snmp-server host 10.0.0.5 version 3 priv cisco-user).

cards.q: What do SNMP views do and how are they configured?
cards.a: They restrict which MIB objects a group can access, e.g. snmp-server view NMSVIEW iso included, then referenced by a group with read NMSVIEW; useful for least-privilege SNMP access.

cards.q: How are SNMP notifications generated and enabled?
cards.a: A destination is set with snmp-server host, and trap generation is enabled with snmp-server enable traps, optionally per category such as snmp, syslog, or config; supported categories vary by release.

cards.q: Why restrict which hosts can reach SNMP?
cards.a: SNMP should not be exposed to every host; an ACL limits which NMS systems can communicate with the SNMP service, keeping it on the trusted management path.

cards.q: How do SNMP polling and notifications compare?
cards.a: Polling is predictable, manager-controlled, and good for statistics; notifications give immediate event delivery without continuous polling; enterprise monitoring normally combines both.

cards.q: What commands verify SNMP on Cisco IOS?
cards.a: show snmp for general status/statistics, show snmp group, show snmp user, and show snmp host.

cards.q: What can show snmp reveal when troubleshooting?
cards.a: Packets received/sent, errors, SNMP versions, requests, responses, and notifications, which helps determine whether the device is actually processing SNMP traffic.

cards.q: Why can an SNMP SET fail?
cards.a: A read-only community, an SNMPv3 user without write access, a read-only MIB object, an SNMP view blocking the object, or authorization/access configuration.

cards.q: How do SNMP and syslog differ?
cards.a: SNMP is for monitoring/management with polling, structured MIB data, and traps/informs over UDP 161/162, while syslog is for event logging with log messages over UDP 514; a device can use both for the same event.

cards.q: How does security compare across SNMPv1, v2c, and v3?
cards.a: v1 and v2c use weak community strings with no encryption, while v3 uses users/groups with authentication and optional privacy/encryption; only v3 is the secure choice, and GETBULK/INFORM are absent in v1.

cards.q: Which port memory should you keep for SNMP?
cards.a: UDP 161 = polling (requests/responses), UDP 162 = notifications (traps and informs).

cards.q: TRAP requires an acknowledgment. Is that correct?
cards.a: No. A TRAP is an unacknowledged notification; it is INFORM that requires an acknowledgment, though both normally use UDP.
